utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.text: And that will be Mr. Barkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.text: Could Mr. Barkovic be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we just -- one issue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What we have attempted to do with the assistance of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And reference is made to the paragraphs in the statement where they apparently are found. They are -- Mr. Russo, I take it that there is no objection against this way of proceeding, which means only that we have tentative MFI numbers assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there is no objection. In fact, I'm not objecting to any of the documents with the exception of one. There ask a page missing from one of the documents. I'm not sure if that is a technical issue that can be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you already mention the provisional MFI number of the document so that the Gotovina Defence is in a position to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's D1599, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the page missing is to be found or is the short document --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe it indicates that page 5 in the original is missing. I have the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if is simply missing and can't be found, that's fine. I won't object to the admission of the document. I just want to make sure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will certainly check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything else? If not, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Barkovic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Barkovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Barkovic, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. I would like to invite to you make that solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. Professor, can you state your name for the record and spell your last name, sir.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mladen Barkovic, B-a-r-k-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor Barkovic, do you recall meeting with the members of the Gotovina Defence team on two occasions, the 30th of April, 2009, and again on 18 May 2009?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you recall signing a statement on the 18th of May, 2009?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could call up 65 ter 1D2693, and if I could hand a copy of that document to the professor with the assistance of the Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you assist Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Professor, I have placed before you a document, the 65 ter 1D2693. Do you recognise this document as the statement that you signed on the 18th of May, 2009?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review this document before you came to court here today?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when we were going through it together, professor, we made certain corrections to this document, did we not, which I would like to go through with you now, beginning on paragraph 10 of the document. And that first 65 ter document that's listed, 65 ter 1D2645, should, in fact, be 1D2648. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And in paragraph -- just taking these sequentially, in paragraph 16, the second-to-last line where it notes the 133rd Home Guard Brigade, I believe you told us that should be the 113th Home Guard Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 113th Sibenik, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In paragraph 20, where you talk about this particular document in the last line, it notes that in the -- in your statement is says 4375 non-commissioned officers were required. And in reviewing the document it, in fact, says 4735. So those numbers were transposed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the final correction is a correction that is not in Mr. Barkovic's document, but it is, unfortunately, in the English. And it's an error that is in the translation on paragraph 23 in the English, the fourth line from the bottom. That -- it refers to a 65 ter and as it's written, it says 65 ter 1 SD 2695. It's correct in Professor Barkovic's original, by the way it should read is 65 ter 1D2659. So the last two digits in the English version have been transposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, subject to the corrections in the statement, does the statement accurately reflect what you said to the Gotovina Defence during your meetings with them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is the information provided in your statement true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Professor, if I examine you today with regard to the same matters that are contained in that statement, would your testimony on those issues be the same?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd move for the admission of 1D2693, which is now been marked for identification as D1583, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, a few questions. The one number in paragraph 23, all the other numbers start with 1D and then a four-digit number. Here we have you corrected the 2695 and 259, but the structure of the number is different to the extent that started 1 SD.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's incorrect. I thought I said something about that. If I didn't -- it should be 65 ter 1D2659, Mr. President. You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I have one or two more questions. When you gave your statement, Mr. Barkovic, apparently you signed it. I see a signature on the B/C/S version on the 18th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you sign it on the day -- was the statement written down in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you -- when did you -- have you reviewed the English version of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We read a draft translation of the original statement before signing it, and then we made corrections to the Croatian versions, whereas -- version, whereas corrections were made to the English version with members of the team over the past couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But have you seen an earlier version of the English translation on the 18th of May or at what point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 18th of May, I saw the draft translation, the draft English translation, but what we were doing at the time was correcting the original Croatian version, which I signed. It was subsequently translated, and I no longer saw that version until a few days ago when I also checked the English version here. Of course, my knowledge of English permits me to notice the minor semantic differences between the two versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, a question for you as well. In paragraph 16, the issue which comes back in the supplemental information sheet as well which has been provided to the Chamber. We see that the translation contains what's appears to be correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the witness signs the original, apparently makes no correction to that. And now, in the translation we find a correction because the answer is not what it should be. That raises some issues as to what a translation means to be. Any comments on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My comment on that is that is why the "[sic]" is there. Because what we did was we literally left in what was in the original so that the reader would know that. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if the original we find the reference to the 113. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But who is translating? You say we. Apparently someone who knows what the answers should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In reviewing the documents, Mr. President, and putting together the package with the appendices, the review reflected that it was the 113th. And we thought for the purposes and clarification of the chamber, while we didn't, of course, alter the original document that he signed, for the purposes of the translation and certainly to assist the Chamber, we thought it would behoove us to inform the Chamber that there was a mistake in that regard and 65 ter 1D2638, in fact, refers to the 113 brigade as opposed to the 133rd. That is why we put the "[sic]" in there because the "[sic]" of course means that -- is literally in the originally, albeit a mistake, is still there. So it was no -- it was merely an attempt to highlight for the purpose of the Chamber that there was a mistake there. We intended, of course, to bring it to the Court's attention in the Chamber; and, of course, Your Honours in review of the actual document itself, the Chamber can see that it is it reflecting [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not commenting on whether the correction is accurately made. I was just wondering to what extent the translation is a coproduction of someone who comments on the content and someone who just translates the language. Apparently it is to some extent a coproduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is. In -- you're absolutely right, Mr. President, and in that sense, that is why we included the "[sic]" signal in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Any objections, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you assign a -- a number has already been assigned to the witness statement. That's D1583 -- well, has been -- Madam Registrar has made a proposal to assign this number to the document. D1583 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and with regard to the balance of the documents that are included in the -- with the -- all the 1D numbers, and I -- a list has been provided to the Register. We would offer the balance of those documents for which the Registrar has tentatively listed -- MFI, I should say, give them MFI numbers of D1584 through D1603.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the puzzle in relation to D1599 has been resolved or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I looked at that document in the original B/C/S and if we see the sequential numbers that are in the upper right-hand corner, they seem to follow each other, and I certainly at the break will consult with Mr. Russo on this, but my courtroom assistant, Ms. Katalinic, pulled it up on the screen, and we can see that the document does, in fact, go sequentially. So I will certainly show that to Mr. Russo from what we found but that's the document that we have that was translated. If Mr. Russo can see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Russo has no objections against admission whether complete or incomplete, if I understand you well. Therefore, D1584 up to and including D1603, as described by Madam Registrar in today's list, which will be entered into e-court are admitted in evidence, and the Chamber would like to hear once D1599 has been verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, I did explain to Professor Barkovic the summary and the necessity and as for the public --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please read the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dr. Mladen Barkovic worked in the Croatian army's Department for Military Education, Training, Research, and Development and the War College from 1991 to 2005. He occupied leading positions in the area of organisation and development of the military educational and training system of the Croatian army and was involved with the officer training provided by the HV, as well as the process through which the HV established various course curricula from 1991 to 1995. According to Mr. Barkovic, the state of the personnel, material, and organisation of the HV during 1991 was extremely weak. Therefore, initially the main tasks of the Department for Military Education, Training, Research, and Development and the War College was to provide support in the process of structurally organising the Croatian army into one unified military organisation as a whole, with an efficient command and control structure being the most important component. To accomplish this goal, among other things, they created an accelerated education and training programme for the lower command levels, squad/platoon/company. With respect to participation in the education and training programmes developed, General Gotovina sent non-commissioned officers and officers from the Split Military District to the courses at the Croatian Military Academy in accordance with the approved quota for the Split Military District. Dr. Barkovic was also personally involved with MPRI and the courses offered and developed with their assistance. Dr. Barkovic was responsible within the HV for coordinating with MPRI in creating training programmes for HV officers and non-commissioned officers, NCOs. The first such training course with MPRI began in late 1994 and was a NCO instructor course, because the HV did not even have enough qualified instructors to train NCOs, let alone enough qualified NCOs. Dr. Barkovic notes that the key to discipline in an army is its NCO level. The NCOs were a significant problem for the HV because the HV was simply unable to properly develop and train this level given the extraordinary circumstances they faced from 1991 to 1995 including lack of time available to train, the selection of soldiers sent for training, the education level of potential NCOs, ongoing military operation, lack of instructors, as well as lack of space and facilities. The international laws of war constituted one of the important elements in the educational and training system of the HV. Dr. Barkovic coordinated with the International Committee of the Red Cross regarding training provided to HV members on the Geneva Conventions, so that the treatment of civilians in military operations would be in accordance with international law. That is the summary of the statement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor Barkovic, we're going cover some topics and not all of the topics in your statement, and we just want a bit of clarity on some of those issues. And turning our attention to paragraph 4 of your statement, Professor, and the first sentence it notes that the state of the personnel, material, and normative organisation of the HV during 1991 was extremely weak. Now, we're going to discuss those and we'll get into the personnel in a bit. But could you give us an overall synopsis of what you are referring to concerning these problems being very weak -- the problems existing and the HV was very weak during the 1991 period. Can you tell us what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that ever since the first democratic free elections in Croatia in 1990, up until September of 1991, Croatia only had a Ministry of Defence without any armed force. All the armed forces contained within the police forces were there, and four Guards Brigades were set up, but there were also a type of "gendarmerie" contained within the police force. It is clear then that the aggression in the summer of 1991 caught Croatia without a Main Staff, without a main command, and without any forces, which in the conventional military sense could be used for any sort of serious defence, let alone any sort of serious combat action, also given the fact that Croatia was partly occupied; in other words, it had parts of it -- parts of its territory which were under occupation. Nobody with any common sense could think that it could achieve this. Another fact that needs to be taken into consideration is that Croatia was under an embargo on the -- on arms imports which meant also an embargo not only weapons but on military training, et cetera. In other words, we were left to our own devices to what we could achieve on our own. If we keep in mind the fact that there was no Main Staff, then it is only natural that no serious regulations existed which would govern the armed forces. The Ministry of Defence was only with modest resources and it was part of the Croatian government, and had to deal with certain operational issues all the way through to the summer months of 1991. That would be the general picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And so, Professor, moving to your actual role in the command structure, what challenges did that present for you and the HV Command Staff in training and educating and bringing the HV up to a professional level?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were many more challenges than possibilities of reacting to them adequately. The first challenge was time. There was no time to mount any sort of training courses. So the first courses which were organised for the personnel holding the positions of non-commissioned officers and commissioned officers at the levels of squads, companies, and platoons were organised for a period of seven days. Subsequently, the courses were prolonged to two weeks, a month, and then two months as well. Over a very short period of time, one had to organise something for the personnel who were active and who could be spared from their duties for a month and in order for them to receive training, which would raise them to a higher level of professionalism than they had before. Another major challenge was that of instructor personnel. The dilemma we were faced with was: Can we spare the personnel who were out in the field, the manning positions, and does their absence, in fact -- is it outweighed by the importance of them being trained in order that they may, in turn, train others. That's how we decided to withdraw people from the front line, in order to take them back there, so they had their firsthand combat knowledge, which was then coupled with the training they received. As for the resources we had at our disposal, we were faced with the same dilemma. Is a piece of hardware more worthwhile when employed for defence purposes on the front line or when used for education purposes within a school? We were far undersourced in these terms of having adequate education instruments. In terms of resource, we also had a lack of space where course attendees would be put up. Croatia had a very high number of refugees and displaced persons, and precisely those who came from Vukovar were accommodated in the premises of the Croatian army, so that they occupied the premises that we were not available to vacate and use for education and training purposes all the way until after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor Barkovic, I've been advised by the Croatian speakers in the audience that they ask you to slow down just a bit, if I may, and I think -- please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe the witness at page -- let me see, page 14, lines 4 and 5, the witness stated where they were accommodated, and I don't think it was picked up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we -- Mr. Barkovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where who was accommodated? The academy or the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Barkovic, it reads now: "Croatia had a very high number of refugees and displaced persons ... of the Croatian army, so that they occupied the premises ..." What premises?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe you missed a line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I missed a line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Line 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was reading from the one screen, and it's not fully consistent with the other one. Let me just check. "And precisely those who came from Vukovar were accommodated ..." Where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the premises of the barracks housing the Croatian Military Academy. There were several such buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That now completes the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Also, staying with that first sentence in paragraph 4, you talk about issues involving the normative organisation of the HV. What are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: When we talk about legislative regulation, we could talking about many areas, of course, but when we're talking about the war and war activities and the use of military force, of course, there must be legislation governing the strategic and doctrinal employment of forces. The next levels are tactics, equipment and procedure. As we go down to different levels of use of equipment and forces, all that did not exist. There was no organised military system at the time that we are discussing, that is, until the end of 1991, when the first regulation started to emerge. All the regulation boiled down to issuing orders to the people who were in the top echelons of the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff, and in technical details, we relied on the literature remaining from the former JNA, instructions on how to use technical and tactical combat resources. One of the first tasks of training was to teach people standardised certain procedures, trained them how to work and how to train other people. So we started from scratch by writing certain instructions that contributed to the process of legislative regulation of the use of military forces. Another aspect of that is the military system, the organisational structure; and as the state developed over time, the military structure began to be more and more regulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's talk a little bit more specifically about the personnel involved in this. And moving ahead in your statement and direct your attention to the beginning of paragraph 5, you note that: "Due to the deficit of officers with competent military education and training, all members of the HV, who previously had military education and training, were shifted on a higher level in the chain of command, while the middle and lower level [sic] command positions were staffed with persons who were about to receive military education and training." Now, can you just elaborate? Exactly what kind of problems are you discussing with regard to the structure of the HV and the challenges that it presented to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Under the circumstances of the aggression, of course, we had to build up a large military force, but we did not have enough equipment or enough weapons, so our main factor in increasing our capacities was mobilising large numbers of men, to create a large number of military units. A military unit is able to function only with a well-established chain of command, and the chain of command consists of people who are able to perform that sort of work. As the military units were created, more and more room was created for promotion. That meant that anyone who had military education and training, be it from schools for active-duty personnel in the former Yugoslav People's Army, or schools for reserve officers and NCOs, or perhaps military knowledge gained in third countries, all such people very quickly gained higher levels of command. That means that former JNA officers were immediately placed in high positions, and at lower levels, command of platoons and companies was vacated. So, in September or October 1991, there was a great need for education and training and longer and shorter courses to enable people to take up these lower command positions, command of companies and platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, again, just for clarity sake, the lower command positions were at the non-commissioned officer, NCO level?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The largest shortage was precisely in NCOs; at lower levels, that is. And commanders of squads were made to be people who showed any amount of ambition, sometimes even against their will, because the position came with increased responsibility; but, at the time, morale was at such a level that such positions were easily accepted. Nevertheless, frequently, we had people in NCO positions who did not even have enough tactical or technical knowledge, let alone ability and training to lead people in a serious military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will get into those issues in a little bit more detail as we move ahead this morning. Before I would -- before we go into that issue, I would just like to touch on a few topics in your statement, preliminarily; and in paragraph 10, you talk about the -- the Home Guard units. And if we could just refer ourselves to two documents D1588, preliminarily, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the sake of the witness, he asked if we could get the hard copy. I have tabbed those out. And if I can just give these same documents to the witness, it may expedite matters, if there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, I take it, Mr. Russo? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Professor, if we could about to your tab 7, which is D1588 in evidence. This is a document from the Split Military District concerning the analysis of training and education in 1994. And if we go to the second page in the English, towards the bottom, in the paragraph beginning: "A semi-peacetime situation ..." It notes in the last line -- I guess the next page in the B/C/S as well: "We know that 60 per cent of the members of our units are expelled persons." Now, you referred to that -- and if I could just go to, yet, another document which is in tab 8, which is D1587. I'm going to just refer to both of these documents, Professor Barkovic, and then just ask you a question about it. And this is on tab 8 of your book.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a report on the training and education conducted in the 15th Home Guard Regiment, dated 19 November 1994. And if we can go to the first appendix of this document, which is seventh page in the English. We note in the second-, third-, fourth-, and fifth-to-last lines in the paragraph, the unit of the 15th Home Guard Regiment consists of 70 per cent of servicemen coming from occupied areas and locations along the front line. And this is on page 7 in the B/C/S. Now, in your statement, Professor, you note, midway through paragraph 10, that the level of their combat readiness and education and training was significantly lower from the level of the professional brigades, and this was due to a multiple of reasons. Well, talk to us about that a little bit, and talk to us about the difference between the professional brigades and Home Guard Brigades, and why this happened and the multiple reasons you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: The reasons result from the differences in the way these units were created, the circumstances prevailing in Croatia as a whole at the time. The first reason is the selection of people. For Guards Brigade, this selection was serious, conducted under well-tested criteria; and it was followed by training for Guards Brigades, initial training, in which officers and NCOs from the Guards Brigade had priority in admission to the Croatian Military Academy, and the Military Academy provided very good training. And homeland units are a different story entirely. They were created on the territorial principle, and homeland guards were joined by people who were willing to defend their country; but they were rather thin in prior knowledge and training. As I said, the capacity of the academy was rather limited and people from homeland guards had a difficult time getting into the Military Academy. Very few people made it, in fact. Those are the three main reasons: Selection in admission; priorities in training; and the fact that they were made up of people, mobilised based on the territorial principle. Almost everyone came from that particular territory. Perhaps not all, but 60 to 70 per cent. We tried to overcome that in this way. The Main Staff issued every year orders on annual training in units, and here we see an example of the order regulating precisely such an effort in a Homeland Guard/Home Guard Regiment. I hope that answers your question why the Guards Brigades were much, much better trained and why they could be used for much more serious missions than Home Guard units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's stay with this training of the Home Guard units. And on this particular document that's on the screen about the 15th Home Guard Regiment, and if we can turn to the next page in the English towards the top, and I will check that that is consonant with the B/C/S. And in this annual analysis of training by the -- of the 15th Home Guard, we note that the top of the page: "With the commanders of battalions, companies and platoons we elaborated the topic international humanitarian law ... "The basic knowledge was provided in lectures, in which we used brochures of the humanitarian Red Cross and international Red Cross." And, Professor Barkovic, before we get into this, if we could please slow down, I think the -- my colleagues are advising me that there has been some difficulty keeping up with the rate of speech. So if we could just try to be a little bit slower, I think that that would be helpful. Now this document, sir, is a review from 19 November 1994. Can you tell us a little bit about your involvement and your experience at the Main Staff in the necessity to instruct on international humanitarian law and what the approach of the HV was.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that very soon after the establishment of the Croatian Military Academy and after it started working in the beginning of 1992, we made contact of the office of the ICRC in Zagreb who helped us with this, and in every course we conducted at the Croatian Military Academy, we organised several hours of lectures by ICRC representatives. Somebody would come from the ICRC and make a introductory lecture and then in the part of the course concerning command and control, there was also a section about desirable conduct in this respect, and explanations were given to soldiers, what is consistent with international Geneva Conventions and what is not. Every year, a new agreement would be signed on cooperation with the ICRC and that became a well-regulated system. This was done not only at the Military Academy but also at the level of units. During training that was conducted, during lulls in combat, during rest, lectures were given on international humanitarian law, so we worked in a two-pronged way, on two levels. A manual on international law on warfare was also translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let take these issues sequentially and first on the timing issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might just have one moment. Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm advised, Mr. President, by Mr. Misetic there was a comment about the time at which this training was going on that has not been picked up in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be page and line number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was at --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was at page 21, lines 15 and 16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- part of your answer relating to the time of -- the time at which this training was going on has not been translated. Could you please repeat that portion of your answer, Mr. Barkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first courses, including that topic we had at the Military Academy, were in spring 1992. And we started 15-day courses in February 1992. So these were the beginnings of the work of the Croatian Military Academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we could just -- on the timing issue, if we could turn to D1592.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Professor, in your book, it's tab 13. And it is a document that is signed by General Bobetko on 14 December 1992. If we could just bring that up on the screen. And in -- in this document, this is it an outline for training, and I turn to the last page where they are talking about -- in the curriculum, other matters. And you note in the reserve time there is a segment for international law of war. Do you see that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, that particular reservation of time, do you know who that time was reserved for to come in and discuss this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After New Year 1993, training began in the command and control school; that is, at a higher level than anything we had done before, and there is the curriculum for this course. And this reserve time was meant for a person from the office of the ICRC in Zagreb to come and lecture. We did not know exactly when he would come, so we set aside time for him to lecture future commanders of battalions and brigades on this topic. They would have firsthand knowledge on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did members of the ICRC, in fact, attend and give those lectures?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they did. They were always very happy to come, and they were very active and even proactive in this effort. They would come an offer their services themselves, and whenever we requested anything, they did even more than they had been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me -- on this same topic, and let me turn your attention to D1601 in evidence, which is a document sent to the ICRC by Major-General Tolj, 25 July 1995. That is in tab 20 of your book, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- Mr. Kehoe, as you about the last document. The number mentioned there, the numbers of hours spent on the topics and the programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since we only saw only, I think, paragraph 11 or 12, what is the total number of hours for the course?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will count that up, Mr. President. I didn't count up the entire hours of the course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw that three hours were reserved for international laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like it know what the percentage is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, we will add that up at the next break or as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On this document, D1601, we note this is a document from the chief of the political administration to the ICRC for the 25th of July, 1995, which sets out a curriculum. But if we could turn to the next page. In the preamble, I'm interested in the time sequence there, Professor, where it notes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could have that on the English on the second page. Yes, that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the continuation of the existing fruitful cooperation between the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and the International Committee of Red Cross in the field of the promotion of international humanitarian law in the Croatian army during 1992, 1993, 1994, the signatory parties to this agreement concur to continue the cooperation in the course of 1995." Do you see that professor?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that the time sequence that you're talking about with the relationship between the HV and the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, definitely. We started in 1992. This document is dated 1995, and it demonstrates a continued cooperation between the Ministry of Defence and our armed forces and the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us flip to D1602, which is tab 14. And, Professor, this is a document from the ICRC, noted the basic principles of the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I don't know if we can necessarily do this. But on the Croatian is it possible to just put the Croatian on and spin it, because there's a date in the column that CLSS hasn't translated that I think is something that the Chamber might want to see. The other way, please. If we can ... there it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Professor Barkovic, this is a basic principles of war document from the ICRC. And could you read out for us the date of the printing on this that is listed in the document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: It says printed in June 1995. The circulation was 10.000 copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Professor, were documents similar to this printed and distributed prior to June 1995 by the HV?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they were done in a short time, based on various sources, usually by the faculty at the Military Academy, and it was distributed to attendees of the courses as part of the courses, the same as was done with all the other training and education material that they would receive during their course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think there is any need to page through this at this point. Obviously, the Chamber can review this document. Unfortunately, the translation that we have didn't have that date on there and I thought it was significant to bring it to the Chamber's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just -- I'm sorry. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can just turn to the training itself and go to your paragraph 7 of your statement. And you note in paragraph 7 that there were -- second to last sentence in paragraph 7: "At the level of some Military Districts education and training centres were established?" Do you see that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you're talking about some Military Districts. Would that include the setting up of these training facilities in the Split Military District, which was under the command of General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can move ahead, Professor, to paragraph 19 of your statement, you reference about midway through that document the centre, and that's a training centre, the centre in Sepurine was focussed at the education and training of soldiers, group squad commanders and non-commissioned officers, squad and platoon leaders. Is that the centre at Sepurine, is that the centre that was set up by General Gotovina for the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was initially set up as the centre for training of the 4th Guards Brigade which was stationed in Split. So, in other words, yes. The answer could be in the affirmative. Subsequently on the initiative of General Gotovina, the centre was expanded and the services of training were provided to other Guards Brigades as well. It eventually, therefore, grew into a centre for the training of NCOs and was integrated into the Croatian Military Academy. In other words, it emerged on the basis of the needs for training of NCOs, and was initially the training centre for one Guards Brigade only and later on expanded to provide its services to all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us continue with this training and basically focus on the Split Military District documentation. And I would like to discuss another document with you, which is 65 ter -- excuse me, yes, 65 ter 1D2781.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason why this document does not have a premarked MFI number is because it has not been on the 65 ter list. I present this to the Prosecution, and I make an ore tenus motion to put it on the 65 ter list. I consulted with my colleague prior to Court and I don't believe he has any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then leave is granted to add it to your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, if we could turn to this document. This is tab 22 in your book. And again that's 65 ter 1D2781. This is a request from General Gotovina on the 20th of April, 1995. Before we go down into the content of this, Professor, I would just like ask you a question about the subject itself. It says: "Request for assistant in building an artillery-infantry training centre for the needs of 2nd strategic echelon of the reserve units of the Split Military District." What units are we talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: This primarily involves reserve forces. The second combat echelon stands for reserve forces, be it mobilised forces or Home Guard forces. They were very similar, according to the tasks they were supposed to perform. What this document clearly shows is that the results -- or, rather, the training courses carried out here were focussed on active NCOs, whereas General Gotovina thought it useful to train the reserve NCOs as well, and wanted a centre to be set up in Split similar to the one set up in Sepurine but this time for the training of the reserve forces and the Home Guard units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if we could talk about paragraph 1 in this document. If we just scroll down a bit under the heading, "Explanation of the request," and -- even prior to that it says: "Due to the substantial needs of the expert training of the non-commissioned officer and officer personnel for the squad-platoon-company-battery levels of command and within the units of the Split Military District (2nd combat echelon), I am submitting ..." It puts the request in, but at point 1 it says: "Given the substantial needs for training and education in the Split Military District in the limited capacity of the Damir Tomljanovich-Gavran training centre in Sepurine and its orientation toward the training of guards units, I am forced to find some other efficient solution for the purpose of raising the level of combat readiness." What was the problem here with the combat -- with the training facilities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Which facilities are you referring to? The ones in Sepurine or the ones in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the ones he is making a request for in this document.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: What is sought here is the premises of the barracks Bribirski Knezovi, Sibenik to be remodelled for the purposes of the training of NCOs, what the problems involved were, who the barracks initially belonged to, and what needed remodel there is something I don't know. The request says that some of the premises should be adapted for the purposes of the training of reserve NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2781.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document will become Exhibit D1604.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying on the -- the training of NCOs that you just mentioned, Professor, I would like to address your attention to paragraph 20 of your statement, where you talk about the importance of NCOs. And then flipping back to paragraph 18, in the first sentence in paragraph 18, you note that: "One of the greatest problems accompanying the development of the HV from the very beginnings until 1995 was the deficiency of the non-commissioned officer corps." Can you explain that just a little bit based on your experience in the HV and your experience in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: What needs to be said first is the fact that the duties of officers and non-commissioned officers fall under two different sets of tasks to be performed by the army. There is a possibility to develop officers from the lowest to the highest rank along one chain, and along the other, the development of non-commissioned officers from the lowest to the highest ranks. It is the NCOs who -- on whom the effective performance of the army depends and very often we would call the NCOs as the backbone of the army, and if they failed to perform, then no officer can make sure that the army is ultimately made operational. We were forced to staff the command positions along the chain of command, and this resulted in the fact that we would very often place the best NCOs to carry out officer's duties. According to the information or the practice of the personnel cadre, if a NCO is placed on an officer's position for three months, upon the expiry of the three months and on condition of good performance, the NCO had to be promoted to an officer's position. This resulted in a chronic shortage of NCOs. This was also caused by the fact that the NCOs themselves saw their future not in a higher ranking NCO position but in an officer's position. The function of the non-commissioned officer corps should have performed within the Croatian army -- could no longer be guaranteed, and this was the problem I referred to in paragraph 18 of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Professor, specifically, what is the practical effect of this lack of trained NCOs when we get down to the squad and platoon level in the HV?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: When we are discussing the directing of a lower ranking unit, i.e., squads and platoons, what is important is that there is personnel there who constantly take care of discipline, proper functioning of the unit, of the morale of the unit, and who make sure that the unit abides by values, from generally social values, through to military values, and to make sure that the unit is behind them 100 per cent. And these are the qualities of a good NCO, who not only gains these qualities through the system of education and training, but is required to have these innate qualities of being able to deal with the individuals with his soldiers, to command loyalty from them, to make sure that, ultimately, the members of his unit will obey his orders, do what is desirable on the desirable values, and will refrain from such conduct as is considered unlawful, irregular, and not desirable. In addition to this, the NCO is authorised to enforce disciplinary measures and punish breach of discipline on the part of his members -- of the members of his unit. The shortage of NCOs on commanding positions of squads and platoons, and even their high fluctuation on these positions had, as its result, lack of discipline and lack of combat readiness in the army, because the NCO has to be the very best soldier of his squad or platoon. He needs to demonstrate his abilities. He needs to command trust from his soldiers which cannot be done through orders but through one's own example. This was the only way of making sure that his men do what a military unit is required to do in times of war and in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying on that topic before we move to a document, Professor, at the bottom of paragraph 5 -- or actually it's several lines from the bottom. Midway through paragraph 5, you note -- of your statement, you note: "As no other personnel resources were available, the establishment of the system of accelerated officers and non-commissioned officers, education and training was the only solution. The situation we found ourselves in was the complete opposite of the normal." Tell us about that. What are you talking about, this complete opposite of normal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: In my answer to the first question put to me today, I said that Croatia found itself in a situation where it had been the victim of aggression and where part of its territory had been occupied. The same applies to this question. When the military organisation was being organised, civilians joined the army and went through various education and training courses, only to be appointed to a certain post. Before they are assigned to their subsequent duty, it was customary for them to undergo certain training. So there was a continued training of NCOs and COs. Following such courses, they would be given a higher rank and a different position. This is what normally takes place in an armed force. However, we had men who were members of military units manning front lines, and it was only from there that they were sent for training. They were trained over a limited period of time - this is something we referred to before - and then our -- upon completed training, they would be assigned to the units they had originally come from. What we wanted to do was to make sure that men who were already performing military duties, upon completed training, were able to perform these same duties but only better. Unfortunately, we had to adhere to this system through to the end of the war. It was only in a handful of cases which involved higher levels, Command Staff schools that they were able to train men before appointing them to a different duty. What our training and education system amounted to was training of men who were already performing military duties, in order to raise their level of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Professor, prior to your -- this will be last question before the break, Mr. President, with your permission. Prior to your joining the HV in 1991, your experience from your statement is with the JNA, and based on your JNA experience, how much time and training was -- was required before a soldier reached the NCO level in the JNA? How many months or years? And did you have that kind of time in the HV?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA educated NCOs through a regular secondary school system. In other words, individuals aged 15 would join a secondary school, and these schools lasted for four years. The first two years were of a general courses, and then the second two-year period concentrated on a given military branch. Once these individuals, aged 18, finished secondary school training, they started serving the army alongside military conscripts; whereas, the -- those who trained the NCOs were very often of senior cadre, had -- in the Croatian army, we had NCO who were senior officers, who had more firsthand combat experience but who had had training for perhaps three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think we're missing some of the translation here, if Mr. Misetic can assist before we get too far down the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that because of the speed of speech, there is an lot missing. So first at page 34, line 3, if we could check the age that the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At what wage did they finish military secondary school training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then the second issue is page 34, lines 5 and 6, something was mentioned. He used the word senior, but I'm not sure that -- I think there may be something missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A reference, at least in the translation we received, is made to senior cadre. Could you tell us whether you added something in this context? Whether that is complete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember mentioning senior cadre. I said that once they completed secondary school education became NCOs and started serving in units alongside conscripts who were their peers. This perhaps is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I belive --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And perhaps it had to do with --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He then continued on and said -- he continued on and said, Whereas in the Croatian arm, and then there was a comparison. And if he could perhaps clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please repeat what you said there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Once I described the practice in the JNA, I compared it with the situation we had in the Croatian army. In the Croatian army, those who received NCO training, were individuals who were of more advanced age and who had more experience of life and combat, in some cases, which made the training easier, on the one hand; but, on the other hand, the training lasted for three months only. There was only one generation of NCOs who had a six-months' training. However, it turned out that we did not have enough time to carry out six months training and had to resort to shorter period training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if this is an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. Your estimate of time is still the same that goes to two hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Approximately the same, maybe just a little more than half an hour when I come back, but I don't think it should be tremendously long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break. Mr. Barkovic, the break will be 25 minutes. And we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to show you a series of three documents before I begin to ask you questions in the spirit of time, just to -- so you can understand exactly the frame of reference of my next questions, and the first one I'd like to look at with you is P -- excuse me, D1595 which is in tab 2 of your book. And it's a document of the 2nd of March, 1994, concerning the training -- NCO training in the 4th Guards Brigade. And the next document, if you can turn to your tab 6, which is D1590.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, we haven't even had the English on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. If we can go back to D1595. My apology, Mr. President. Let's go back to tab 2 before we go to tab 6 and scroll down a little bit in the English and get the full breadth, at least the first page. We note at the bottom of that page: "By conducting training every day, motivate NCOs to preserve the reputation of members of the 4th Guards Brigade in any situation and transfer their positive influence to other members of the brigade and the HV." Attached to that, we can just -- if we can just go up a couple of pages, to page 7 in the English and 7 in the B/C/S. You note the training objectives, at quarters of the way down, teach them the basics of military psychology that will enable them to work with people in a better way, train others, and behave appropriately in crisis situations. If we can scroll up a little bit at the top of that page, you talk about one of the goals being the disciplined conduct of the NCOs. Turn to the next page in English, page 8 in the English, page 8 in the B/C/S. And the subjective goal, 2.4.3.1, talking about service regulations: "The objective of the subject is to teach NCOs to carry out obligations correctly and learn about disciplinary measures in the HV." And then it discusses the actual topic itself. And again if we go to page 13 in the English and 22 in the B/C/S. Talking about factors, command -- military command and control includes, among other things, discipline morale, et cetera. If we can move ahead to tab 6. Tab 6 in your book, which is D1590. This is an order from General Gotovina dated 7 January 1995, pursuant to an order of the Main Staff regarding the training of non-commissioned officers. We note in the first paragraph the order is to organise, provide training to commanders of squads, platoons, companies and battalions of Home Guard Regiments of the Split Military District, and it gives a particular location. We note in paragraph 2 the purpose of the seminar. But in paragraph 3, Professor, you notice the squad levels, and we have a series of numbers. Are those numbers which add up to 100, are those at the NCO level training for individuals at the NCO level? You have to say orally. I --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: NCO level, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with these two documents in mind, I'd like to turn to yet a third document. That takes us yet a bit further chronologically. The last document was 7 January 1995, and I'd like to take you to D1596, which is a document drafted by General Gotovina. You mention in paragraph 20 of your -- on tab 5 for you, paragraph 20 of your statement, and it is dated 16 February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can bring that up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tab 5, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a document. It notes proposal, selection, deployment and control of non-commissioned officers in the HV and is sent to Minister Susak, General Bobetko, and others including General Roso. And if we can turn to the next page to get the date of this. And starting with the first sentence, General Gotovina writes: "I have repeatedly warned high-ranking HV officers of the staffing problem in the HV at various meetings and briefings, including, naturally, those at the Split Military District [level] ... I last did it in the analysis of the order, work and discipline in the HV in 1994, which was carried out, as you know, in the 113th Brigade in Sibenik on 9 and 10 1995." Moving down in paragraph -- excuse me, just staying with that paragraph: "On that occasion, I directly related the order, work and discipline in 1994 to the staffing issue, namely, the issue of a specific group of staff that we call non-commissioned officers." Just moving down one sentence: "Trying to find a solution to the problem and improve the order, work and discipline in the long-term, I have come to realise that it should be necessary to make some radical changes in the overall attitude towards the non-commissioned officers in the HV. The present attitude is unsatisfactory. "If we claim, as we justly do, that non-commissioned officers present [sic] the pillar of the army, then we should adopt a different attitude towards this pillar in all segments of life and work." Now, Professor, you're familiar with this document. And can you give us some explanation: What's the problem here as late as February 1995, with regard to NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the hitherto interpretation of this statement, we clarified in which way we trained and educated NCOs. I'll repeat briefly. That, from 1993 onwards, there has been in existence a NCO school with a capacity of between 200 to 300 attendees at a time, once in three months. That makes less than a thousand men per year. Another school for guards NCOs was active in Sepurine, and I would like to emphasise that the connection when I said that NCOs were constantly promoted to officers rather than to higher NCO positions, this problem was recognised very well by Gotovina - probably he was familiar with it from his prior career - and he took steps to make sure that NCOs see their prospects in climbing through the NCO structure, not straight on to the officer level. So the system of recognising and appreciating NCOs and their importance and achievements in building up the army, as well as recognising their renown in the armed forces was established. That is an element that supports the role of the NCO structure in many other armies. I don't know what other details you might be interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can go into some of the details, and one of the details is General Gotovina mentioning at paragraph (a) of this document, and I believe that's page 3 in the B/C/S that -- and you mention this in your statement at paragraph 20 that there -- the NCO level's at a 60 per cent strength. And if we turn the page again to the time-frames, and this is page 3 in the B/C/S, page 3 in the English, under the numbers there, what training for non-commissioned officers means to us can best be seen in the fact that more than 80 per cent of the non-commissioned officers in the Split Military District are from the Homeland War, where they obtained their ranks through wartime services. "The training currently offered at the HVU is short and has even been reduced from six to four months." Now General Gotovina has got concerns about the level of NCOs and also the time it is to training. Now, what was the position of the Main Staff on this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that these are facts that are very rational and that prevailed at the time in the Military District of Split, and they tell us at least two things. First of all, there was a shortage of NCOs; also, because NCOs were given ranks and promoted to officers. And the second thing is that schools and the Military Academy had insufficient capacities and there was a need to change something about that. As for the reactions of the Main Staff to this communication, I don't know what it was, but I know that in 1994 a number of programmes was started, together with the American company MPRI, these programmes were for the democracy transition assistance, and one of the main tasks of that team was to size up the situation, and they also noticed the same problems that General Gotovina writes about here. We had to create a special structure of training and promoting the NCOs within the NCO structure, along the lines Mr. Gotovina describes here. I believe, therefore, that the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff had recognised the problem even a bit earlier and reacted by opening this project with the MPRI which was a long-term project and could not deal with the problems immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last issue raised by General Gotovina on the bottom of page 3 and page 4 in the B/C/S, under the heading of the advertising for non-commissioned officers' duties, promotion to a rank and control in the service and profession in general. He noted: "The fact of the matter is ..." Do you see that, Professor? Page 4 of the B/C/S, page 3, under the subheading C.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The fact of the matter is that the ranks of non-commissioned officers in the HVO are not popular, and, it must be also said, we have done little (if anything at all) to make them more popular. Today, most ... men see themselves as officers, a few of them as non-commissioned officers, mostly only on a temporary basis [sic] but this rank in the army is not just a rank, it is a service, a profession, a military specialty that cannot be done without." Now, that particular focus, I mean, how did you understand what General Gotovina was trying to bring about with that comment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I understood it the way it was written, and I believe it was written very precisely and accurately. It is a fact that the job of the NCO is a particular speciality. They are not authorised to command units and operations. They are authorised to manage a group of people they were -- that were given to them by officers. But they are responsible for building a team with whom they would perform these tasks. They live together with this team, they train it, and the best units in these units are NCOs. And if the NCO only thinks of how he would be promoted to an officer, then it's not good. This is not a short-term job. It's a long-term job to build up a team like that. I think what we have behind this sentence is a profound knowledge of the structure of the military organisation and the way military jobs should be professionally performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the last page of this document which is page 5 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S, under the conclusion. In the conclusion, and I'm referring to the last sentence: "Having competent non-commissioned officers in these positions means, without a doubt, having before organised work and order, better discipline and far fewer unusual incidents, but also far better combat readiness for these [sic] units." How do these competent non-commissioned officers that General Gotovina refers to play into better organised work and order and, most importantly, better discipline and far fewer unusual incidents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Definitely, a NCO is a man who lives together, breathes with his soldiers. The number of people he managed is five to ten, depending on whether it's an infantry unit or a different unit. That's a system within which one man can effectively manage such a number of people. He can be in constant conduct and communication with them. All members of his units can see what he is doing, how he is doing it, and he is able to set an example of how things should be done. He discusses with them values and value judgements about what is good and what is bad, ethical aspects. Through this work, an awareness is built on belonging to the unit, on what is good and what is bad conduct; and once that has been built, the members of that unit, even if the absence of the NCO, if they are struck by an idea to do something which is irregular, are aware that they are surrounded by people who would not approve, and that serves as a deterrent. And thus, the work of the NCO contributes to building a conscious discipline among members of the army, based not only on fear from punishment but also on the awareness that one should carry oneself in the same way as the others, whether the NCO is there to control it or not. That is the role of the NCO in creating a consciously disciplined conduct of the members of the unit who would then be apt for being deployed and employed. As for extraordinary incidents, that means anything that is considered to be unacceptable and prohibited behaviours, starting from shirking duties, such as guard duty and other duty, to going AWOL. That's the way in which the quality of the NCO corps can be linked with everything that contributes to the quality of an army, in terms of readiness and ability, and discipline, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Professor, given your answer, I put to you some of the evidence that has been presented to this Chamber concerning possible improprieties by HV members, and I would like to go through a series of documents and have you respond to them. The first being D204. I'd like to show you three documents and then ask you a question at the end so if you could bear with us as we go through those. D204 is a document, an order from General Gotovina, 10 August 1995, approximately four days after the end of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, this is document from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And "Subject: Order, on compliance with military disciplinary measures based on the information from the areas liberated by the HV, the analysis thereof, and in order to prevent theft of property undisciplined conduct and to save ... lives I hereby order: I prohibit arbitrary movements of the HV members in the liberated areas without the knowledge of their superiors [sic]." Turn to paragraph 2. "Take all necessary measures and fully engage in the implementation of the military disciplinary conduct and the maintenance of order in the area of responsibility, and prevent arson and all other illegal acts. Take resolute measures against anybody who conducts himself in an undisciplined manner. Signed Major-General Ante Gotovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could turn to P -- next document, P1140.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is an order from Colonel Mladen Fuzul, 19 August 1995 heading: "Due to the observed breakdown of order and discipline and for the international reputation of the Republic of Croatia, I hereby order: 1, establish control [sic] in all units and immediately take measures against torching -- against the torching of buildings and the killing of animals; 2, take disciplinary and criminal measures against responsible [sic] individuals?" Let us turn to one last document on this subject before we begin to ask questions on it, than would be P918.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could put that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a document that is -- comes out of the Split Military District political affairs section, penned by Captain Mario Tomasovic and the subject is: "Warning." And we go to the second full paragraph. We're talking about items after Operation Storm: "However, because of the irresponsibility of individual soldiers, non-commissioned officers, and officers, who compromise the Croatian army and state through their inappropriate conduct and acts, this success has been partly brought into question." The success that we're talking about in the prior paragraph is that brought about by Operation Storm. Next paragraph: "For this reason and following the policy of the Supreme Commander Dr. Franjo Tudjman as well as the instructions of the defence minister and the political administration of the defence ministry of the Republic of Croatia, it is necessary to immediately prevent the following: 1, the continued torching and destruction of facilities and property throughout the entire liberated area [sic]; 2 ... killing of live stock; 3, confiscation of property; 4, inappropriate conduct toward remaining civilians and prisoners of war ... especially towards members and soldiers of the peace forces." Professor Barkovic, we have talks about this morning about any number of topics, the formulation of the HV in training, the existence of Home Guard Regiments, the training facilities for NCOs and lack thereof, and the need for training in international humanitarian law, yet on the -- after Operation Storm, there are orders and reports such as this that are in the record of this Trial Chamber and this case. If there is this training, Professor, and if these orders are being given by General Gotovina down to its soldiers, how do these things come about? How did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: My answer can be based only on indirect knowledge. However, it can quite clearly be explained why this situation came about. Let's take the example of a -- of a Home Guard Regiment, which reaches an area and liberates an area where its members hail from. They come across their own properties which had been razed to the ground; whereas, their neighbours, who had lived in the area until Operation Storm or even continued living there thereafter, had their properties intact. This required a high degree of strict control to make sure that such individuals did not engage in misdeeds. Evidently, it was not possible for us have that degree of control, and one of the most immediate reasons is that even those who were not taught -- even those who were taught the provisions of international humanitarian law and who had undergone training still were unable to restrain the heightened emotions on the part of their soldiers. We know that not many people need to breach discipline or to be undisciplined in their conduct in order for great damage to be inflicted. This is why it was very easy in such a situation where the lower NCOs and lower-ranking NCOs and lower-ranking officers were few. We saw what the conditions for education and training were in place at the time for individuals to engage in the sort of conduct, which is mentioned as prohibited in this document. The third problem is the chain of command. The singleness of command is one of the principles, where the superior will issue orders to the first subordinate officer, who, in turn, will issue orders to his first subordinate officer, and so on. In other words, these orders had to go through a number of levels down the chain of command, and that each of these levels, there was a risk of noise, as it were, which resulted in poor understanding of these orders, especially if the lower levels of command, in particular the NCOs, were not sure as to how and in what way these orders needed to be adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, specifically, based on the training that is given, when soldiers are out, for instance, looting, who is the first person in authority that should be there to stop that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what we were discussing today, it's the NCOs, for two reasons. One, because they are constantly present with their soldiers; and, second, because they need, with their own presence, to command loyalty and respect and to make sure that their soldiers know what proper conduct is. So they were -- they are the first ones who should notice any such conduct and make sure that such conduct is not engaged with. In other words, it is the NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, based on what you've written and told us today, why did they not do it successfully?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: There are several reasons for that. One is the number of trained NCOs. Very often the NCOs who were present in the field had not gone through training for the reasons we explained. The second reason is that many individuals regarded the NCO duties as only a springboard to higher officer levels. That would be the two reasons which proved sufficient; whereas, the third reason is the absence of such a NCO corps, which would, along the chain of command, not only on one level but along the entire chain of command, make sure that discipline is enforced.
