utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just being back, sir, to your second reason and I want you to play this into what we said. This is on line 20: "The second reason is that many individuals regarded the NCO duties as only a springboard to higher levels." Can you explain that a little bit in your explanation as to why they didn't stop this inappropriate conduct to the extent that it occurred?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the objective need to develop a large armed force over a short period of time played into such a situation. Because the army ranks grew, the NCO -- the NCOs were pulled higher up, were promoted to higher levels. Where one NCO went, the others followed. There were attempts to develop a large NCO corps only in 1994 when the combat situation calmed down somewhat, before the military operations. By that point, a contract was signed with the MPRI company, and one of the tasks was to develop the NCO corps which would function the way I described it should have. Another effort was the development of NCO schools, because the NCO schools existed in the navy, as well as in the aviation --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to this NCO duties as only being a springboard to higher officer levels, how and why did that affect discipline on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: What arose was the problem of sufficient time. In order to build up a team which shared an awareness of belonging to a unit, time needs to pass. The NCOs need to have time to pass with the members of the squad or the platoon they are in command of. If that period of time is short or if the NCO does not expect to remain at that position for a long time, he will not be able to create that feeling of oneness with his members, if he knows that he will very soon move on to higher positions. So it takes a long time to build a cohesion between the NCO and the unit, which will ensure that the military unit involved is successful in its activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might have one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Barkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Ms. Higgins, any questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No, questions Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you have some questions, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Thank you. Mr. Barkovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Russo. Mr. Russo is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Before we move into more specific areas, I want to be clear about something at the beginning. You're aware that HV soldiers, not just members of the Home Guard Regiment but members of the professional brigades, committed crimes, such as looting and burning in the immediate aftermath of Operation Storm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly I have to say that I don't know who the perpetrators were not by their names, save for what I was able to read in the newspaper, mentioning individuals and their units. I don't know more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about specific individuals. What I'm asking you is if you are aware that soldiers, for example from the 4th or 7th Guards Brigades, or any of the Home Guard units that were involved in Operation Storm, you are aware that they committed looting and burning in the immediate aftermath of Operation Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can I take your testimony, your -- that is your witness statement plus the testimony that you have given here today, can I take that to mean that you attribute those crimes to a lack of NCOs. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: That is one of the reasons. You know that in any community, regardless of what sort of education and training it had or how it was brought up by the family, there is always crime. We know that the motives of such criminal offences can always be varied, and that is the case in this specific circumstance we're talking about it -- we're talking. I know that what forms military discipline in an army is the presence of the NCOs who are in command of some 10 to 30 men, and they are the backbone and the guarantee that extraordinary incidents will not occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were shown some documents by Mr. Kehoe regarding orders that General Gotovina had given against looting and burning and for the maintenance of discipline and a few other documents along the same lines. Are you aware that similar orders were issued to members of the Croatian army, that is both professional Guards Brigades and Home Guard Regiments, prior to the operations in Grahovo and Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: This fact is not known to me. However, since I'm familiar with the workings of the army, it is only natural that -- and we were able to see one example here from Colonel Mladen Fuzul, that the commanders receiving such orders immediately forwarded them down the chain of command. So I suppose that this was the case, although I hadn't heard of such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Professor, indeed, it's not necessary for a commander to specifically issue an order not to commit a crime; isn't that right? That's part of the code of military discipline, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: But when a commander, in fact, does issue that order, not to engage in, for example, looting and burning, that is supposed to someplace some special emphasise on it for the troops; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It most probably means that such incidents occurred, that they were analysed, and that it was concluded that it called for an additional intervention. For this reason, these steps were taken to additionally emphasise matters that needed paying special attention to. Following any extraordinary incident, the army conducts analysis and takes measures regardless of the fact that the same matter had been regulated previously. This is the case in traffic incidents, in brawls, and in many other cases I have knowledge of. So I'm not surprised that as soon as first indications emerged of improper conduct, additional measures were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And when the additional measure of issuing a specific order is taken, you'll agree with me, won't you, that it's necessary to ensure enforcement of that order, and equally important that when the order is disobeyed, that someone who disobeys it is disciplined for that; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes. However, it seems to me that the incidents which occurred fell into the category of criminal offences, in respect of which soldiers did not have powers to react but to pass them on to those officers who engaged in criminal offences. They could only impose disciplinary measures for minor breaches of discipline, which are not crime. In other words, commanders could take disciplinary measures and report criminal offences to those whose duty it was to investigate into them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if we could check page 53, the sentence starting on line 11 and ending on line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Starting with, "Generally speaking, yes." That portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "However, it seems to me ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Barkovic, I will read to you a portion of your evidence, of which we're not fully certain that it's completely or accurately translated. I must add to this that your speed of speech creates these kinds of problems and it not the lack of competence of our interpreters or transcribers. Let me read to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, I will try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read to you the relevant portion of your answer. You said: "However, it seems to me that the incidents which occurred fell into the category of criminal offences in respect of which soldiers did not have powers to react but to pass them on to those officers who engaged in criminal offences." Well, especially the last part of the answer comes a bit as a surprise. Did you intend to say those officers who would deal with criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I meant -- first of all, instead of soldiers it should read commanders. Commanders are the ones who can issue disciplinary measures against soldiers, and their second obligation is to report criminal offences to those who should investigate them ex officio. This is at least my understanding of the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you in relation to this, say I'm a platoon commander or I see someone putting fire to a civilian house. What am I supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] React instantly and stop it, because you are in the position of a commander, who can tell him what to do and whatnot to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the platoon commander cannot prosecute or convict that person instantly. A certain procedure of investigation and prosecution and punishment is required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, you have to react immediately when you see the offence happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say, Stop immediately, and he doesn't do that. What do you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the story of military discipline again. A soldier has to obey his superior. The superior can either react by force himself or order two men nearby to seize the person and stop that conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then do what with the person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military police must be called, and the person must be turned over to them, together with the report on what he had done, and then the case is in the hands of the military police. One should not forget that military commanding officers are busy with things happening at hand, and such incidents are in well-organised and well-disciplined armies still an exception, not the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let's just assume that the military police is not nearby. You will have to wait for two hours before you could expect them to be there. What do you do with the person? Do you keep him under control by force and wait until the military police arrives; or do you ... which would, to some extent, obstruct further [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, the person has to be kept under control from then on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, along the lines of the Presiding Judge's questions, enforcing and maintaining discipline is the responsibility of every kind of commander from the lowest level NCO, all the way up to the highest general; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we must bear in mind the possible range of control, because we -- when we are talking about the commander of an operation group --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me -- I just want some focussed answered to my question. We'll explore the matter a bit further. Now, you indicated during your direct testimony that when a NCO fails to perform his duties that operational -- that officers are unable to put together an operational army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is linked to the possible range of control. A NCO controls five to ten men, which is much easier than controlling 30 or 40 men, as an officer has to do. It is even harder for a company commander who cannot keep 150 soldiers under constant control. That's what I meant. I'm not saying it's not their obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, when a NCO doesn't do his job, when he doesn't prevent soldiers from looting and burning, it becomes that NCO's immediate superior, it becomes his responsibility, then, to enforce and maintain discipline, not only on the -- on that NCO's subordinates but on the NCO himself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if, as I'm sure we all recognise, the lieutenant or the company commander is unable to stop the immediate conduct that's happening, for example, looting and burning, it's not the matter, right, that he simply forgets about it after it occurs, right, he has to follow up and make sure that what he witnessed and what he knows went on is addressed through the military discipline system; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And going back to what I was asking you about at the beginning of the examination, the fact that orders similar to the ones that Mr. Kehoe showed you about preventing looting and burning, the fact that such orders were given prior to operations in Grahovo and Glamoc, you're aware, aren't you, that those orders were not effective to prevent looting and burning in those operations; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: It's normal that in every order, according to operation procedure, there is an item regulating treatment of civilians, prisoners of war and the property in the area designated, and it is normal to emphasise, that once again, in every order, although it is in the appropriate regulating documentation. Or perhaps I did not understand another part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- let me make it a little clearer. I'll just ask it again. Are you aware that the orders not to loot and burn were not effective to prevent looting and burning by soldiers in Grahovo and Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if these things happened, it's obvious that the orders did not attain their goal, or, better to say, were not executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that when an order such as that is issued and it is not effective and it is not followed, that it doesn't behove the commander to simply reissue the same order and hopes it gets obeyed the second time.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Measures of control and inspection must be taken, personal control at one's own level and two levels below, see what's happening, why it's happening, learn the lessons, and get to the bottom of that and then achieve appropriate conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, along the lines of your answer, some of the goals of the code of military discipline are primarily to correct an errant soldier who breaches discipline; secondarily, to set an example to other soldiers that they should abide by the code of discipline; and, thirdly, to ensure the proper functioning of the chain of command; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So when a soldier commits a breach of discipline such as the looting or burning of civilian property and suffers no consequence from that, then the aim of correcting him, first of all, is not achieved but also the aim of teaching others that that soldier's conduct is not appropriate also fails; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, General Gotovina was aware of the shortage of NCOs and also the lack of training of the NCOs who were in place; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And he was also aware of the problems that his soldiers had with discipline, before Operation Storm; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not really aware of that, but I suppose he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, in particular, he was aware of the fact that the soldiers that he was going to use for Operation Storm were inclined to loot and burn Serb property; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't say what he thought about that. He probably had reason to suspect there might be undisciplined behaviour, but his mission was so serious and so great that he had to reckon with certain risks in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understand your answer. First of all, if I put it to you that General Gotovina was aware that members of the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade, as well as members of the Home Guard Regiments who participated in the operations in Grahovo and Glamoc, he was aware that they burned and looted Serb property in those areas prior to Operation Storm, you're not denying that or disputing that, are you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not disputing that. I'm saying he could have thought along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you are aware, aren't you, that even in the midst the burning and looting that was going on there Grahovo and Glamoc that General Gotovina ordered preparations for the awards and promotions of, among others, the NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Although it is common knowledge that after every military success awards are given to those who contributed to that success the most, those are necessarily not the same people. Some people can be rewarded, while others can be punished. I don't suppose he awarded or rewarded those who had committed misdeeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please -- I'm sorry, Madam Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit P71. And if we could go to page 49 in the English and page 25 in the B/C/S. And in the B/C/S, we can focus on the left side of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you see here, Professor, where it indicates -- reported by the 72nd Military Police Battalion: "In Grahovo, all the soldiers except for the 1st Croatian Guards Zdrug and the 3rd Battalion of the 1st HVO Guards Brigade members took part in setting fire to houses."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, if we could move to page 73 in this exhibit and B/C/S page 36. That's on the left side of the document in B/C/S. Focussing on the enter row on the bottom, Professor, where it indicates that Minister Susak has seen the area, and he indicates how disappointed he is in the burning and looting and notes that it is especially noticeable in the areas of the 4th and the 7th Guards Brigades. Now if we could go to page 71 in the English and page 53 in the B/C/S. If we could move a bit down in the English, and it's on the left side in the B/C/S. Sorry, are we on page ... I'm sorry, I need page 53 in the English and 27 in the B/C/S. Is that where we are? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, you can see here the entry for General Gotovina. He says: "It is important to prepare for the promotion of soldiers, non-commissioned officers, and officers, as well as for giving awards." Now, Professor, you've seen that the report was that all the soldiers, with the exception of the ones from the 1st Croatian Guards, Zdrug and the 3rd Battalion of the HVO Guards Brigade, all of them were participating in burning. We have here General Gotovina preparing for awards and promotions of, among others, the non-commissioned officers. Do you consider this to be reasonable for General Gotovina to do and do you consider that to be a reasonable measure to prevent that kind of conduct from occurring in future operations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] If you pull out -- oh, excuse me. [Interpretation] If we connect in the entire military situation and in war operations these two facts, I don't think that's the right thing to do, because a military operation is much more complex than the incidents that occur during that operation, and nobody ever knows everything that happens during a military operation. I'm not talking about this particular one now but about military operations in general. But what is logical is that when a military unit has done a big military job, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I just want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. I would ask that the witness be able to explain his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the question was about this particular situation, whereas the witness wanted to explain, apart from this particular situation. Would you please first answer the question, and if there's anything you would like to add in relation to that, which is not directly linked to the question, please feel free to do so. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my mind, connecting these two facts - on one hand, there was burning, and, on the other hand, there were promotions - is not specific enough. I suppose that General Gotovina did not envisage promoting and rewarding those individuals who were guilty of such things. That's what I suppose. If that is so, then I think his reaction, as a military commander, is appropriate, that successful, good individuals be promoted and awarded. On the other hand, I expect that disciplinary measures would have been taken against those guilty of disciplinary infractions and prosecutions started against those who were guilty of criminal offences. But what exactly happened, I think you can only check from the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, let me deal with the second part of your answer first. First of all, I agree with you that one would expect disciplinary measures to result from the conduct that we've just read about in the operational diary. But I'll put it to you, Professor Barkovic, that there was no discipline for looting and burning in -- as a result of the acts in Grahovo and Glamoc. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think, sir, that this is a misrepresentation of the record concerning disciplinary measures -- that the rise in disciplinary measures. If Mr. Russo is going to put information to him, he should put the facts to him about the rise of disciplinary measures taken in the Split Military District --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you can object, but then to say what, in your view, the proper presentation would be, of course, would be to take over and then we could expect Mr. Russo to tell the Court that you're misrepresenting the -- Let's -- Mr. Russo, you are aware of the concerns expressed by Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't, first of all, believe it is very fruitful use of the court time for me to put my exhibits to the witness, and tell him what I think they mean. I can certainly give the Court the exhibit numbers to which I'm referring to make those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question started that you agreed with him on a certain matter. Apparently there is the issue. Whether you agreed with something that is the testimony of the witness, yes or no. Would you please -- Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one last matter, and this goes to the 90(H) issue concerning discipline. I mean, these issues concerning discipline and what happened in Grahovo and Glamoc were never put to Mr. Milas by anybody from the Office of the Prosecutor. And this is an instructor -- when a person who was in the military police was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to address matters one by one. There's no read to read it, to go through all the documents. But I think the witness clearly testified that if crimes are committed, that disciplinary action should be taken against them. And apparently, Mr. Russo, you agree with him on that part, which is ... and then put your question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Barkovic, this Trial Chamber has heard evidence and has received evidence that for the months of -- for the entire quarter which encompasses the operations in Grahovo and Glamoc as well as Operation Storm that there were no disciplinary actions taken against members of the 4th Guards Brigade, 7th Guards Brigade, or any of the other units that participated in the operations in Grahovo and Glamoc. No disciplinary measures were taken against them for looting or burning houses. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that before, and I agree with you that measures should have been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you would also agree with me, wouldn't you, that if measures weren't taken after Grahovo and Glamoc to redress the looting and burning that it created a further risk of the same conduct continuing in the aftermath of Operation Storm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I'm looking at the clock. Two questions. The first, when would be an appropriate moment to have a break; second, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now is an appropriate time for a break, Mr. President, and I believe I will need at least the next session, possibly more, but I will try to finish in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, we had a witness here recently who offered some testimony about General Gotovina's role in the training of NCOs, and I wanted to run that by you and determine whether or not it's accurate. Is it true that in order to cure the deficiencies at the NCO level, that the leadership of the Croatian arm looked principally to General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So you wouldn't say that General Gotovina was leading the effort or had the responsibility for the training of the NCO corps?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I saw his initiatives, starting from the training centre of the 4th Guards Brigade and its evolution, into a training officer for all the Guards Brigades, to the document I just saw, the initiative to round off and create a NCO corps, and I -- on the basis of that, I can state that he was inactive -- active in these matters, and but I cannot state that this was a task that he was given from the top military echelons. It only goes to show that he was privy to the relevant matters and that he made an effort to create the -- the NCO corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we check the interpretation, page 66, line 8, the third word.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter said he was active, not inactive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, the training academy or school that General Gotovina created to train the 4th Guards Brigade, that was back in 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: The 4th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, NCOs are not -- well, they're responsible for more than simply enforcing and maintaining discipline; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The NCOs are responsible for several matters. The two matters we discussed, to a lesser extent, is the training of soldiers in technical and tactical skills. In other words, the maintenance and use of weapons, and tactical activity in terms of coordination and use of weapons. These are the two matters. And the third matter is the building of morale, discipline, and common values shared by the entire team, how to create a team out of a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And they're also responsible, aren't they, for ensuring that the orders for a particular combat mission are carried out, and carried out effectively, by their unit.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Even more than that. They are the best and the first soldiers to personally take part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And when an operation is conducted successfully and effectively, it's an indicator, isn't it, of the effectiveness of the NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that Operation Storm was an operation which was conducted quite well.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you would also agree with me, wouldn't you, that the system of command and control functioned also well during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, if General Gotovina -- first of all, let me ask you this: Do you believe, or do you know whether General Gotovina considered the command and control system to function well during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think that he had firsthand insight into the strengths and weaknesses of the system. I don't know what his personal opinion of it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you a few documents about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We can begin, Madam Registrar, please, with 65 ter 1776.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: While this is coming up, Professor, I'll just let you know that that is an analysis conducted by General Gotovina, dated 16 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if we could please go to page 14 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S, looking towards the top of the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you'll see that General Gotovina indicates here: "The command and control system in Operation Oluja functioned relatively well in the conditions that existed."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Before I move on to the next document, Mr. President, I would like to offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is there a question about this document, or is this bar tabled, I mean, what's the procedure? I mean, bar table, we generally -- I look at it ahead of time and then we make an agreement about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was a question put to the witness in relation to the matter which is covered by the document. But there seems to be no direct link between the witness apart from that you put a question on the same subject to him, so that would make more or less a bar table document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, it will be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will take a look and get back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2585.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could now have Exhibit P2559.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And while this is coming up, Professor, I'll let you know that this is also an analysis done by General Gotovina. It is dated 15th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, we will be looking for page 5 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S. If we could go a bit down in the English. If I could have a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you see, Professor, where it indicates at number 1.2, it states that: "The 4th Guards Brigade, 7th Guards Brigade and 81st Guards Brigade, the HV 113th" -- I believe that's anti-armour or infantry, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the 126th --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Infantry, infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: 126th Home Guard Regiment deserve special attention in respect of appropriate command and control. Now, if we could go to the last page. That's page 8 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S, you will notice at 2.10 General Gotovina again is making reference here to proposals for accommodations for officer, non-commissioned officers, and lower ranks as a result of the operation. He is clearly pleased with the way the operation was conducted --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I just object to the commentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know what is objectionable about that. I'm putting to the witness that General Gotovina believes that the operation was satisfactory and was pleased it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is not in the document. I mean, the document says proposals for accommodations for officers, non-commissioned officers, and lower ranks by segments included in the attack operation will be submitted later. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently, Mr. Russo -- Mr. Russo, what portion were you exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That is the portion I was referring to, Mr. President. Perhaps I could follow up with a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier I also noticed that -- that preparing and proposals are not yet final decisions on giving awards and -- but please proceed, put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, it's not typical in the Croatian army, is it, to propose or consider awards and commendations for officers and non-commissioned officers of whose conduct you are not satisfied; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Although, I must state, that I can't see either in this document or in the earlier documents that it was those same persons who had committed crimes, who were being considered as the recipients of awards of -- or commendations. There were tens of thousands of people who took part in the operation, and, of course, not all of them committed crimes. There must have been a number of them and they are not the same people, or at least, I hope and believe that they are not the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, since you brought it up, you did notice when I showed you the operational diary the report by the 72nd Military Police Battalion that all soldiers with the exception of those who were named --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- were taking part in the burning of houses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Objection to that, and I let it go before with -- and I will address this. We're talking about a particular area and counsel has yet to determine whether the soldiers that are being discussed are HVO soldier are or HV soldiers in that town at that particular time. Now I will address [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In re-direct, but my objection is the foundation of the question that the witness ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The foundation for the question is the report as it was shown to us, which refers to units and it apparently is the 4th and the 7th Guards Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doesn't say that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, it says all units with the excepting of two. I'd like it know, first of all, whether or not it is in dispute that the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade were in Glamoc and Grahovo on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is in dispute. It is in hot dispute, absolutely. Where exactly they were when this report comes in. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You do recall the portion of the operational diary that I read where Minister Susak expresses his disappointment and indicates that the burn is particularly noticeable in the areas of the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you also --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, that is exactly what we're talking about. We're talking about an area where troops are moving in and out. Are we saying that the 4th Guards Brigade is there when this takes place? There is no establishment of that in the question, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. We then have perhaps -- at least it's in one of the exhibits that we have just seen. Reference is made to the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade. Let's try not -- we have to understand the -- the evidence in its entirety, and if for every document we would go to every detail, 4th Guards Brigade, did that mean every member of the 4th Guards Brigade or would that mean -- I mean, you reach a level where we have to -- to look at the documents in its context, and even if that would now and then, Mr. Kehoe, and that happens with all parties, result in a -- in a summary which is only for 99 per cent correct and not for the full 100 per cent, then we'll look at it in its entirety. Mr. Russo, you are aware of the concerns expressed by Mr. Kehoe. Would you please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, if General Gotovina is satisfied with the functioning of the command and control system during Operation Storm, then the lack of NCOs and the lack of training of the NCOs really wasn't the issue, was it? I mean, the correct functioning of the command and control system manifested in the appropriate combat actions and in the NCOs carrying out their responsibilities in that regard; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't necessarily see that the two facts are directly linked. The fact of the matter is that General Gotovina and all the other officer, including the Main Staff of the armed forces were full aware of the state of the armed forces. Therefore, the expectations matched the actual state of affair when it come to the armed forces and not against an ideal situation, where everything has been achieved. So I suppose that the satisfaction is based on what could be expected of an army organised as it was. It was impossible for the army to be fully manned by trained officers and NCOs. It -- its performance was the way it was. In other words, I could not accept an opposite conclusion. It was -- in relative terms, that the judgement was made, based on the level of organisation and training. Otherwise, it would have constituted a too great a simplification to conclude something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, what I'm putting to you and regardless of the standard that General Gotovina set by which to evaluate the soldiers' conduct during the operations, whatever standard he set, it's still appears, don't you agree, from what's been indicated here that he was satisfied that that standard was met by the units which participated in Operation Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: When a mission operation achieves its military objectives, the commander must be satisfied with the outcome. He cannot be dissatisfied. However, at the same time, he can observe all the shortcomings, which is through the various analyses conducted post-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And when you conducted an analysis post-operation and singles out units for special recognition for command and control, you would agree, wouldn't you, that that is a recognition of the proper functioning of the NCOs in their tasks?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which units he commended, because at item 2.10 which you referred me to in relation to your question, relates to proposals for commendations and promotions of individuals, i.e., individual officers, NCOs, and soldiers, and not units. In other words, I don't have any knowledge about awards being given to units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think you may have misunderstood me, Professor. I read to you from -- this is Exhibit P2559, where in his 15 August analysis, General Gotovina gives special recognition in respect of command and control, a that's a quote. He gives special recognition in respect of command and control to 4th Guards Brigade, 7th Guards Brigade, the 81st Guards Brigade, the 113th Infantry Regiment, and the 126th Home Guard Regiment. Now you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that that means that the NCOs in those units did their jobs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think I answered the question. It is difficult to make such a simplified statement. The -- the special recognition had to do with their achievement of objectives, and not anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the achievement of objectives, Professor, is, in fact, one of the obligations of the NCOs, isn't that right, to see that the objectives which they are given are, in fact, achieved by their units.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: One has to bear in mind that the objectives are set in such a way that they are realistically achievable with the manpower one has at one's disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, doesn't this show, Professor, that it's not a problem of lack of training or a problem of insufficient NCOs. When the NCOs have a job to do that they're interested in doing, they get it done. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: In one of my answers, I explained that the NCOs have three types of tasks, some of which they can achieve better, and others poorer. It is down to their technical and tactical levels of training, the spirit, morale, and discipline of the unit. These objectives could have been achieved if the level of training and tactical activity was good, even if the morale or discipline was not. These are two separate issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I'll put it to you that the HV soldiers, and that means both professional guards and Home Guard Regiments soldiers, were less interested in preventing or refraining from burning and looting than they were about attacking Serbs and Serb property in general. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: In an offensive military operation, the enemy needs to be destroyed and pushed out of the area, which needs to be captured. This is objective number 1, 2, and 3. Of course, one always has to make sure that this is going done in keeping with the international conventions and regulations, but it cannot not not be an objective of the same level as that of the military objective. We have to be serious. War is not a game. It is not the primary objective of a war not to destroy a house. If the house conceals an enemy, it has to be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to show you something from the war journal of the 6th Home Guard Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could have 65 ter 5709. And if we could go to page 4 in the English and the B/C/S. And I'm looking here for the entry of 5 August 1995. I'm looking right at the top of the English from where it begins: "At 0850 one can hear echoing over the radio links Evo Zoreeva Dana Evo Jure I Bobana the dawn has come, the daylight has come, Jure and Boban have arrived. Obobdina has fallen."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document before I ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could now have 65 ter 5706. If we could look at section 2. Where it indicates: "Our troops performed a fair number of combat actions during the day; specific task of the Operation Kozjak 95 was worked off till 0850 hours when Jure and Boban was heard from Obobdina."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor Barkovic, you are familiar with the song, "Evo Zore Evo Dana."

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber -- well, let me just put it to you, it's an Ustasha song; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It's a song that glorifies the exploits of the black legion.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, war crime, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to the Trial Chamber, I mean, given the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, exactly the line what the song apparently glorified, due to overlapping speakers, is not known to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apology, Mr. President. That was the black legion. Jure and Boban were black legion commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Legion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, given your knowledge of the training and education of Croatian soldiers, why do you believe soldiers would think it appropriate not only to play this song but to report the fact that they played it in two official HV documents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I really don't know why. Oh excuse me. [Interpretation] I really don't know. Of course, I do not approve of it. We have always had problems with attendees of courses with regard to the state policies and the distancing from all the events during World War II, the quisling and the age, et cetera. However, perhaps due to family experience and family traditions, these matters did persist. Why certain individuals used this as a code for communication is a question that needs to be put to someone else. I'm not the right person to answer this. What I can say, because I was on the Main Staff and in the academy, that we have always placed things in their right place, and we have always responded properly to this. General Gotovina, who was also present in the academy, always reacted to this and never joined such extremist positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I take it, then, that General Gotovina was present when these kind of sentiments were expressed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, you indicated that: "General Gotovina, who was also present in the academy, always reacted to this and never joined such extremist positions." What was it he was reacting to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Reacted is a wrong word. What I wanted to say was that we discussed the conduct and positions of soldiers and through these discussions, I was able to conclude that he disapproved of such positions. This was from conversations we had in our official dealings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I want it be clear about this: You discussed with General Gotovina the fact that soldiers at the academy were expressing extremist sentiments against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certain individuals did. When we discussed the matter, we took proper positions in relation to this, and General Gotovina upheld these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And what is it that you mean, that you took proper positions in relation to this? What exactly happened to soldiers who expressed those kind of sentiments?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Through a subject called homeland education, they received lectures, they heard lectures on the history of the Croatian state, including explanations about what the independent state of Croatia was from 1941 to 1945, about the policy of the Republic of Croatia, that it was written in the preamble of the Croatian Constitution, what it was based on, et cetera. All these things were mentioned in the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you would agree could me, wouldn't you that in light of the training and the expression by the faculty at the academy that broadcasting, first of all, "Evo Zore Evo Dana," and then writing down the fact that you have done so would call for some form of discipline?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I've got one last area I want to go into with you and that is in reference to -- I'm sorry, before I move on, I would like to tender into evidence the 6th Home Guard Regiment war journal. That's 65 ter 5709, and the OG Sinj daily report, which was the last exhibit, 65 ter 5706.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 5709 will become Exhibit P2586; and 65 ter 5706 will become Exhibit P2587.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and -- If the Court is interested, Mr. President, I do have a document which I don't want to show to the witness, I will bar table it, which contains some of the lyrics to the song. If the Court is interested, I can tender that. Otherwise, I will simply move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness testified about the kind of the character of the song. We don't need the lyrics. Unless there is any dispute on whether this is a proper characterisation about what the song is about. There seems to be no dispute about that. Then the Chamber can do without the lyrics. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you now a bit about MPRI and the training that they gave to members of the Croatian army armed forces. Now, you discuss a bit about the training provided by MPRI and General Gotovina's support for that training; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And this was training that included not only some instruction on the Laws of Armed Conflict but also about how NCOs were to enforce those principles inside their units; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you said it ... not only some instructions on the Laws of Armed Conflict. What's the basis for this part of your question? I do not find in paragraph 22, if you were referring to paragraph 22 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I was not making reference to any particular piece of evidence, Mr. President, but I don't believe it is in dispute that this was at least a portion of the training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, from some of the documents we received today and I took the break to glance through them, I have, as a matter of fact, no specific references to the laws of war as found by me, but I may have missed something. But looking at the late 1994 curriculum it goes into details as swimming and running but not laws of war. So, therefore, I'm just, at this moment, well, not sharing with you, but telling that you I do not find it in the statement of the witness, and I have not found it, until now, in Appendices 14, 15, 16 and/or 17, which are referred to in paragraph 22. So, therefore, if your line of questioning continues on this basis, I have difficulties in understanding what exactly the basis is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Perhaps I will clarify with the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether or not the instructions given, the courses given by MPRI contained some elements of instruction on the Laws of Armed Conflict?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of the subjects related to command and control, that was always included, although it was not specially emphasised here. For higher levels of education, such as the staff school, the curriculum included a special topic through which it was taught. Otherwise, it was taught through topics related to command and control and through practical training, drills, exercises, situation exercise, et cetera. It's true that there is no explicit reference in the curriculum of the MPRI. There is no explicit references to international humanitarian law. Those were curriculums for lower officer levels and they deal with desirable conduct, and that, again, is related to command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's true, isn't it, that the soldiers who were sent to these MPRI courses were not exactly interested in them and, in fact, felt free to simply stop attending?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. First of all, it's not soldiers who joined these courses but those who had already completed the Croatian NCO school. So the course for NCOs was mentioned in the document is -- was, in fact, an advanced course. It built on the knowledge gained in the NCO schools. And if you look at the MPRI programme, it is geared towards making these people better communicators, better instructors, towards building the appropriate spirit. It was not a combat programme. No combat skills were included, because, among other things, that was under embargo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. Professor, I'd like to finish this before -- we only have a few minutes until the end. You did answer my question though, at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter 7276. And just in order to move through this a bit quickly, this is a document which is a letter -- the cover page is a letter to Defence Minister Susak from Major-General Kresimir Cosic regarding a request by a Major Werner Ilic to be transferred back to the Split Military District. I take it you're familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That will save a little bit of time. Now, this is a letter which indicates that Major Ilic wanted to leave the MPRI class, return to his unit, and that that was, in fact, proposed on his behalf and I believe approved for him to ultimately do that. What I'm more interested in is Major Ilic's conduct and in regards to that, in explaining to Minister Susak the circumstances General Cosic attaches to his letter, a letter from General Griffiths who was the head of MPRI mission in Croatia about the conduct of Major Ilic. So if we could move to page 4 in the English and that's page 3 in the B/C/S. And if we could look at paragraph 5, it indicates: "I later learned that Major Ilic had requested relief from his assignment and reassignment to his former unit. I do not personally know his reasons for leaving, since he never discussed the issue with me, but I know that he was unhappy with the DTAP programme and unsure of the programme's contributions, as he viewed the programme. Frankly, I am not familiar with situations where a junior officer's inflated view of himself and distorted view of his surroundings, are permitted to drive the personnel assignment process."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to page 1 in the English, which is also page 1 in the B/C/S, and look to the third paragraph, where General Cosic states: "The Major Werner Ilic was included in the project MPRI with the task to adjust the programme MPRI DTAP as much as possible to the needs and priorities of the army which is at war. In that sense, I personally spoke several times with the Major Ilic, expressing full support for his work. Unfortunately, the Major Ilic gave up." I'd like to move now to the top of the next page in English and to the middle of the following paragraph, which is on the same page in B/C/S, where General Cosic goes on to state: "The reasons for his dissatisfaction of the existing condition, we can consider justified but his approach to resolving the existing problems, we consider unacceptable. Leaving the work [sic] place without approval, or by threatening to jump out of the window, I consider inappropriate behaviour of an HVO -- of an officer of HV (I am sending the opinion of the General Griffiths in the attachment). Probably, our expectations of the Major Ilic were too high. Therefore, I suggest that he should return to his original unit." And a bit further down he states: "After consulting General Gotovina, Brigadier Sundov and a Colonel Kresic, you will have adequate proposal prepared." Now, Professor, it seems - and correct me if I'm wrong - that General Griffiths' concern was, in fact, the reality that Major Ilic's sense of what he wanted was able to drive the personnel process. And by simply not showing up at MPRI, he was able to return to his unit, as he wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC
utterances.text: So Ilic came as a young soldier from the United States into Croatia. He displayed great ability in his first combat activities. He was quickly promoted to the rank of major. That's usually a rank you get in your 30s. He got that rank much earlier. He came from an environment which was very dynamic, where he had worked in open spaces, that's how he was organised mentally and physically, and he had come to stay as a teacher, as an instructor, in the DTAP programme. He did not come to attend, to learn. He came to become an instructor. In -- he was not happy with the classroom work during that course, and he exploded mentally, if I can put it that way. He made two outbursts, one of which was this jumping through the window, which was completely unreasonable, of course; and the second time was when, without asking me or General Griffiths, he wrote directly to the chief of the Main Staff, as we can see, Mr. Cosic does not approve but he also appreciated that the man is unwilling to be a teacher and an instructor and he should not be forced to. We don't want unwilling instructors and that's why he says, that in consultation with personnel officers and Colonel Kresic, he will prepare a proposal what to do next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, there will be another Chamber sitting this afternoon in this courtroom. Therefore, we will not able to go beyond the time any more than we have already. Mr. Kehoe, may I take it there will be some questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means, Mr. Russo, that we cannot finish today. How much time would you need more?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Probably less than ten minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Probably less than ten minutes. I would first like -- I'd first like to instruct you, Mr. Barkovic, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether the testimony you gave already today, or whether testimony still to be given tomorrow. I'm quite confident that we'll finish tomorrow within approximately not more than an hour, I would say, altogether. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom, because we adjourn for the day and we resume tomorrow, the 14th of July, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of July, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
